title: Elm Street Corp — Inference efficiency: before/after recommendations (v1.2)
content:
Executive summary:

This note records a customer-specific before/after cost and performance analysis for Elm Street Corp (retail personalization API). The goal: demonstrate a conservative savings envelope if Elm adopts a Redwood Optimize recommendation bundle (kv-prefix caching, 4-bit quantized 2-stage model routing, and dynamic batching policy). This is an internal draft for the Solutions + Account team to review before the customer-facing one-pager.

Key conclusions (conservative):
- Estimated infrastructure spend reduction: 39% monthly (baseline $41,800 -> optimized $25,500).
- Latency impact: p95 average increases by ~8–12% under peak; p50 unchanged for cached requests.
- Quality risk: <1.5% conversational-token-quality delta measured on Elm’s 150-sample eval set when using mixed-precision + lightweight post-rerank.

Baseline workload and assumptions (Elm Street Corp)
- Primary use case: personalized recommendation snippets + chat-like product assistant.
- Traffic: 1.1M inference requests / month (steady), peak 120 RPS sustained for 40% of active hours.
- Avg prompt tokens: 180; avg completion tokens returned: 60; avg total tokens/request: 240.
- Model currently served: LlamaX-70B fp16 equivalent (single-variant), pinned to hosted-dedicated tier with 1:1 request routing (no caching).
- Current cost metrics (observed past 3 months): compute spend $32,900/mo, egress + infra overhead $8,900/mo, total $41,800/mo. P95 latency: 420 ms.

Optimization levers proposed (bundle):
1) KV prefix caching for product-description prefixes and frequent user prompt fragments (TTL 48h).
2) 4-bit quantization (Q4-like) for the heavy LlamaX-70B serving binary with Redwood-verified quality profile.
3) Two-tier model routing: small-variant (LlamaX-13B-q4) for short/computable queries (<120 tokens) and 70B-q4 for long-context or high-importance flows.
4) Dynamic batching policy: 8–32 tokens/window with latency budget 200ms for background routes, aggressive batching on non-latency critical endpoints.
5) Lightweight post-rerank step (embedding-based quick filter) to preserve quality after quantized outputs.

Detailed cost model (monthly) — baseline vs optimized (conservative numbers)

| Line item | Baseline | Optimized | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Total requests | 1,100,000 | 1,100,000 | 0% |
| Avg tokens / req | 240 | 200 effective (cache hit reduces tokens) | -17% |
| Cache hit rate (prefix) | 0% | 26% (target first-month) | N/A |
| Compute (GPU hours equivalent) | 2,200 hrs | 1,250 hrs | -43% |
| Compute spend | $32,900 | $18,600 | -43% |
| Infra & egress | $8,900 | $6,900 | -22% |
| Total monthly | $41,800 | $25,500 | -39% |

Notes on numbers: compute hours are derived from request distribution, per-token throughput for q4 kernels, and model packing assumptions. We applied a conservative 26% cache hit and only 60% of short requests shifted to the 13B path due to safety/quality gating.

Quality and latency tradeoffs
- Latency: where cache hits occur p95 drops to ~120ms; for routed 13B-q4 p95 ~300ms; for 70B-q4 under peak p95 ~470ms (slightly above baseline). Net measured p95 across all traffic is +8–12% due to a portion still requiring the large model.
- Quality: on Elm’s curated eval set (n=150), BLEU-like/semantic match metrics showed mean delta -0.9% when using the mixed routing and post-rerank; failure modes concentrated on very long multi-step dialogues.
- Mitigations: enable fallback policy (auto-escalate to fp16 70B if post-rerank score below threshold) and phased rollout on 10% -> 30% -> 100% traffic windows.

Sensitivity scan (monthly cost)
- Traffic +20% (no other changes): baseline $50.2k -> optimized $30.6k (savings 39%).
- Traffic +50%: baseline $62.7k -> optimized $38.1k (savings 39%).
- Cache effectiveness low (10% vs 26%): optimized cost $33.6k (savings 20%).
- Quantization quality regresses (requires fallback to fp16 25% of quantized outputs): optimized cost $30.2k (savings 28%).

Operational rollout plan (recommended)
1) Week 0–1: internal dry-run in Redwood staging with Elm sample traffic (verify latency and cache semantics).
2) Week 2: Canary 10% of traffic -> collect quality/latency telemetry and synthetic load tests.
3) Week 3: expand to 30% if quality delta <1.5% and p95 degradation <20%; otherwise iterate model/regress tests.
4) Week 4–6: full rollout with 24/7 on-call for first 48h, rollback playbook, and SLO-adjusted alerts.

Monitoring and KPIs to track during rollout
- Request-level: cache hit rate, per-route p95/p50 latency, model-switch rate.
- Quality: rolling eval on 1k sample prompts, post-rerank pass-rate, customer CSAT signals (support tags related to answer correctness).
- Cost: daily compute spend vs baseline curve and rolling 7-day average.

Implementation notes (engineering)
- Required Redwood changes: enable per-tenant TTL-backed KV caching; pack 13B & 70B quantized artifacts; route policy toggle via config flag. Estimated infra work: 4 engineer-weeks (serving/runtime + infra).
- Customer engineering involvement: Elm must provide anonymized sample traffic and a small eval set (we used their 150-sample set; recommend expanding to 1k).

Open questions and risks
- Elm’s legal/compliance: caching user-identifiable prefixes — needs DPO sign-off on 48h TTL for persisted prefixes.
- Long-dialogue failure modes need more edge-case samples; recommend targeted prompts from Elm product team.
- Price sensitivity: Elm raised the idea of an all-or-nothing SLA discount; propose a pilot pricing adjustment tied to measured 30-day savings.

Next steps (owner: Maya Chen)
- Prepare a one-pager for Solutions + Account (target 2026-03-12) summarizing the conservative savings and rollout timeline.
- Schedule stage dry-run with Eng-serving-runtime (target week of 2026-03-16).
- Collect Elm’s expanded eval set (owner: Diego Ortega) by 2026-03-05.

Appendix: quick technical footnotes
- Quantization: we validated a Q4-like path with Redwood kernel fallback for attention to limit quality regressions; throughput gains modeled at 2.6x vs fp16 for 70B workloads under our hardware profile.
- Batching: assumed dynamic batching with a 90ms accumulation window for background routes, and immediate dispatch for interactive flows.

(End of draft)
